1:
How far the word brother reaches is settled by the next clause. Gill argues that it cannot mean kinsman, since the law goes on to suppose the man may be not merely at a distance but unknown, and denies that it is limited to the commonwealth or church of Israel either, because what is enjoined is a piece of humanity the law of nature itself requires. Wesley reduces it to two words, any man's. Henry reasons from the lighter case to the heavier: the kindness commanded in Exodus toward an enemy is here required much more for a neighbour, though he were not an Israelite, the law being consonant to natural equity. Keil alone keeps the narrower sense, glossing the term as fellow-countryman, and treats the passage as a further expansion of the older law on how a neighbour's property was to be regarded and preserved. Gill adds that the two animals named stand for every other creature a man has, camels and asses and the rest.

What the finder must actually do is spelled out in stages. Keil sets them in order: bring the beast back to its owner, and if the owner lives at a distance or is unknown, take it into your own house or farm and keep it until he comes to seek it. Gill says the same, keep it until it is owned and then restore it. Henry allows an alternative, that strayed cattle be brought back either to the owner or to the pasture out of which they had gone astray, and then gives three separate grounds for the duty — pity to the very cattle, which while they wandered were exposed; civility and respect to the owner; and justice, since it is doing as we would be done by, which he calls one of the fundamental laws of equity.

The repeated prohibition is the phrase they linger over. Wesley glosses it twice and the two glosses do not agree: to hide oneself is to dissemble, to pretend not to have seen, to pass by as if one had not looked — or else, he allows, it means to hide the thing, that is, to conceal what was lost. Clarke takes only the first sense and presses it hard: the command is not to keep out of the way of affording help, nor to pretend one saw no occasion to render a neighbour any service, and he names the standing example of the breach, the priest and the Levite who saw the wounded man and passed by on the other side of the way. Gill turns to the last case in the series and reads it literally, of a beast fallen under its burden and unable to rise with it either of itself or with the help of those standing by, so that the passer-by is required not merely to refrain from injury but to put his hands to the load.
5:
None of them thinks the verse is about clothing alone. Gill renders the first term as any instrument of a man, any utensil he uses in his trade and business, so that the thing forbidden is a woman appearing as though employed in it; and he sets the law against the Egyptian custom the Israelites had lately left, where, as Herodotus reports, the women traded abroad while the men kept at home. Keil goes wider still, insisting the word signifies neither clothing merely nor arms only but every kind of domestic and other utensil. Clarke narrows it the other way: since the noun properly means a man of war, he thinks armour is intended, and denies outright that a simple change of dress can be meant, since in those countries the dress of the sexes had little to distinguish it and every man wore a long garment, so that passing for one another would have been impossible. Gill allows the armour rendering too, on the authority of the Aramaic version.

What the law is for divides them. Clarke grounds it in a cult, the women appearing in armour before Venus, whose worship the Canaanite one strikingly resembled. Henry reports that reading as one opinion among several, but himself puts first the preservation of our own and our neighbour's chastity, and adds a second sense in which the law forbids confounding the dispositions and affairs of the sexes as well as their garments. Calvin will have nothing to do with the idolatry and makes it modesty in general: God anticipates the danger that women should forget modesty or men degenerate into an effeminacy unworthy of their nature; garments are not in themselves of much importance, but propriety is prescribed not only for decency's sake but lest one kind of liberty lead at length to something worse — and he quotes Juvenal's line asking what modesty a helmeted woman can show, who has fled from her sex. Wesley lists the same reasons at once — that the sexes God has distinguished not be confounded, that all appearance of evil be avoided, that suspicions be cut off — the practice carrying a sign of effeminacy in the man, of arrogance in the woman, of lightness in both.

Two of them qualify the prohibition rather than defend it. Henry allows the thing to befriend a lawful escape or concealment, while calling it justly questionable whether it may be done for sport or in the acting of plays. Wesley draws the same line in the verb, that the prohibition covers what is done ordinarily or unnecessarily, since in some cases it may be lawful, as to make an escape for one's life.

The argument from nature is made twice and briefly. Henry says nature itself teaches a difference in their hair, and by the same rule in their clothes, which ought not to be confounded either in ordinary wear or occasionally; Ellicott says only that this is one of the things of which we may well ask with the apostle whether nature itself does not teach us. Henry then defends the smallness of the law, observing that these statutes seem to stoop very low and take cognizance of things mean and minute, which men's laws do not, since the law takes no notice of trifles — but that because God's providence extends to the smallest affairs his precepts do the same; and being found among the things of God's law they are to be accounted great things.
6:
Why the mother must be let go is answered five ways. Keil grounds it in the affectionate relation of parents to their young, which God established even among the animals and which was to be kept just as sacred. Calvin makes the precept a supplement to the sixth commandment, God instructing his people in the law of kindness; he grants that regard was had to the breed, adds that a sitting bird, being very lean, is not wholesome food anyway, and rests the weight on humanity — if there be one drop of compassion in us it will never enter our minds to kill an unhappy little bird which so burns with love toward its young as to be heedless of itself. Clarke offers the conservation reading first, that destroying both young and old must soon fail the breed and go ill with them in the end, then looks for the humane precept and finds it in a distinction: the young never knew the sweets of liberty, the dam did, so the young may be taken for any lawful purpose but the dam must not be brought into captivity. Wesley divides the reason between the parties: partly for the bird's sake, which suffered enough by the loss of its young, since God would not have cruelty exercised toward the brute creatures, and partly for men's, to restrain their greediness, that they leave the hopes of a future seed for others.

Two of them go to the rabbis, for different things. Gill fetches the limits of the law: it does not touch nests purposely made for fowls kept at home, so that geese and hens nesting in an orchard fall under it while doves kept in the house do not; and he reports the rule that if a man lets the dam go and she returns, even four or five times, he must let her go again — a thousand times, one authority says. Ellicott fetches an argument instead, a Talmudic comment that no duty in the Law with a promise of reward attached lacks the resurrection of the dead hanging thereby: both the honouring of parents and the liberty of the nest promise prolonged days — the case being put of a son who obeys both commands at once and dies in the act.

The parapet is explained from architecture. Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin and Wesley all note that the roofs were flat and walked upon — Clarke adding that men went up for the fresh air, to converse and to sleep — so that without a balustrade a fall would be fatal and, as Calvin puts it, every house would often have been a house of mourning. Keil calls the thing a rim and sets the law under the same head, that human life was still less to be exposed to danger by carelessness. On the penalty they are severe: Calvin notes the injunction carries its own denunciation, that the house would be defiled with blood if anyone fell from an uninclosed roof, and Clarke says that if a man neglected a sufficient defence and another's death followed, the owner must be considered in the light of a murderer. How far the rule reaches then divides them. Gill narrows it by rabbinic definition to a house to dwell in, not a granary or barn, and not to any house under four cubits square. Wesley widens it by equity as far as it will go, reporting that the Jews hold themselves obliged, and we with them, to fence or remove everything by which life may be endangered, such as wells or bridges, lest any perish through our omission.
9:
The four rules are read as one rule. Calvin has no doubt they are supplements of the First Commandment, all condemning strange medleys, and finds the proof in the reason subjoined: God declares the produce polluted if there be divers mixtures, so that nothing else is demanded but that they cultivate purity. He notes that the Hebrew word properly means to sanctify and is here taken for the opposite. Ellicott reads the same word the other way, as marking the crop forfeit rather than common, and notes how crops became common at different times, the year's corn freed by the wave-sheaf. Wesley concedes the precepts are in themselves small and trivial, given for that time and state of the church as instructions in greater matters and to commend simplicity. Keil groups the four together and heads what follows as laws of chastity and marriage, higher and holier still.

On the seed the question is what counts as sowing. Gill restricts the law to corn and herbs and not trees, which is why a fig tree may stand in a vineyard, and again to what is sown by design: if seeds fall from a man passing through, or are carried in with dung or water, or the wind carries his seed behind him, it is lawful.

Why the ox and the ass may not be yoked draws four answers. Clarke reports the general supposition that such mixtures were superstitious and prefers a physical reason: two beasts of different species cannot associate comfortably and so never pull pleasantly, every farmer knowing how much the comfort of cattle depends on pairing those that have an affection for each other. Wesley makes it purely ceremonial, the one beast clean and the other unclean, God teaching men to avoid pollution by the touch of unclean things. Ellicott takes all the grounds at once — humanity, the step and pull of the two being so unlike; cleanness, the ox fit for sacrifice while the ass had to be redeemed, so that clean and unclean must not till the holy land together; and the apostle's unequal yoking. Gill supplies the agricultural background, that asses were used for ploughing in some countries — Pliny reporting African land which in dry weather no ox could plough but a mean little ass could after rain — and offers as a reason the fear of breaking the law against gendering cattle of diverse kinds.

The last two rules are handled quite differently. On the mixed garment Gill reports that the rabbis confine the prohibition to what is spun and woven, and corrects Bochart by name for denying such stuff to the priests, since the blue and purple and scarlet of their vestments were dyed wool. Ellicott works from the prophets instead, noting that priests in Ezekiel are forbidden woollen garments in their ministry, since they shall not gird themselves with anything that causes sweat, and that the inner tabernacle was of fine linen while the outer coverings were of hair and wool. On the fringes Ellicott makes them a memorial, a mourning for the man executed for sabbath-breaking and a reminder to do all the commandments — adding that it was this fringe on our Lord's garment that the sick laid hold of and were healed. Wesley agrees and adds a public profession of nation and religion, by which they might be distinguished from strangers. Calvin will have none of it: the fringe was an accessory to chastity and a matter of modesty in dress, since the thighs were then uncovered and an open gown left a door to improprieties, so that God would have the flaps drawn together by ties. Gill records that some made this a law of its own to be kept at night, and that Aben Ezra opposed them warmly and called them liars.
13:
The case is read as a manoeuvre, not a grievance. Gill takes it of a man who marries, cohabits, then dislikes his wife and wants rid of her by this method. Henry supplies the motive as lust after another woman and sets the passage under the seventh commandment, a restraint laid by a penalty on fleshly lusts which war against the soul. Calvin says the passage tends to the exaltation of chastity and finds three objects in it: that a husband should not unjustly reproach an innocent young woman, that one who had in fact been defiled should not escape by pretending otherwise, and — a third he marks specially — that parents should be admonished to watch over their children more carefully.

What the evidence was, two decline to investigate in the same words. Henry says the learned are not agreed on the proof by which the accusation was shown false, that it is not necessary to enquire, and that those for whom the law was intended no doubt understood it; Wesley repeats the judgement almost exactly. Clarke will not leave it there. He grants that the usage argues a roughness of manners ill comporting with the refinement of European ideas on so delicate a subject, reports the attempts made to read the law metaphorically, and dismisses them as failing so perfectly to establish anything like probability that setting them out would waste his time and his reader's; a similar custom, he notes, is observed elsewhere, and where girls married at ten or twelve the case was perfectly possible.

The penalties are counted and explained. Calvin numbers three for the calumny — stripes, a hundred pieces of silver to the father, and a standing bar on ever putting her away — and takes the stated reason, that he brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel, to show God the protector of young women. Henry lists the same three and explains the last by the alternative: he might have divorced her by the law's permission, but then must have given her her dowry, so that if to save the money and do her greater mischief he destroyed her good name instead, it was fit he should forfeit the permission for ever. Gill turns that into arithmetic, the fine being exactly double the dowry he was trying to avoid paying, so that the penalty is measured by the motive; and the chastisement, he notes, was not reproof but blows, the Aramaic versions and the rabbis alike rendering it that they shall beat him. Henry draws the general rule that the nearer the relation, the greater the sin of belying them.

How much of this falls on the parents is a running theme. Gill says they would act partly for their child's credit and partly for their own honour, being in danger of contempt for having educated her ill; he observes that the father and not the mother speaks, and reports the inference that a woman is not allowed to speak before men, adding that if the parents were dead those who had brought her up were to undertake her cause. Wesley gives the same reason for the money going to the father, that the reproach fell on his family and himself, such a miscarriage being ascribed to his evil education. Gill reads the place appointed in the other case the same way, the door of her father's house being chosen for his greater disgrace and as a punishment for his neglect. Calvin, facing that case, anticipates the objection that the punishment is too severe and answers commercially: a false sale of a field or house is accounted a crime, and so is the uttering of false money, and therefore one who abuses the sacred name of marriage for deception much less deserves pardon. Keil marks the turn plainly: in the other case, if the man's words were true.
22:
On the first case they are brief and agreed. Gill notes only that the law respects adultery and repeats an earlier statute. Clarke draws a historical point from it, that in the most ancient of all laws adultery was punished with death in both the parties. Calvin calls the verse a political supplement showing how greatly God abominates the offence, since he denounces capital punishment against it: marriage being a covenant consecrated by God, its profanation is in no wise tolerable, and conjugal faith is too sacred to be violated with impunity, since it is an act of horrible perfidiousness to snatch from a man's bosom the wife who is as his very life, or at any rate half of himself.

The next case turns on betrothal being counted as marriage, and they justify that differently. Calvin grounds it in the promise given: the severity is extended further because she has plighted her troth, and it is a token of abandoned incontinency for a woman's mind to be so alienated from the man she is betrothed to. Gill grounds it in law rather than sentiment, distinguishing betrothal from marriage as the Jews did, with time generally passing between the two, and listing the three ways a wife was obtained — by money, which was the most usual; by writing, which had to be done before witnesses and with her consent; and by cohabitation. Keil sets out the structure instead, two cases or really three: whether the woman was betrothed or not, and if betrothed, whether the thing happened in the town or in the open country.

That last distinction is the hinge, and it works by presumption. Wesley states the first side flatly: she did not cry, and is therefore justly presumed to have consented. Gill fills in the reasoning for the other side — the field is a circumstance in her favour, since had the act been by agreement they would doubtless have betaken themselves to some other place, and her crying may be concluded from that circumstance and from her own declaration, which the man could neither gainsay nor disprove. Calvin puts it as probability, that one who has been ravished is not criminal and a woman forced in a field is absolved because it is likely she yielded unwillingly. Wesley then supplies the principle underneath, that the cry is in such a case to be presumed, charity obliging us to believe the best till the contrary is manifest.

The comparison the law itself draws is the one they dwell on last. The text sets the case beside a man rising against his neighbour and slaying him, and Wesley glosses the likeness exactly: not an act of choice but of force and constraint. Clarke takes the same comparison as a measure of value, holding that a woman's honour was reckoned equally as precious as her life, so that the same punishment was inflicted on the ravisher as upon the murderer — and he observes that the offence is considered in the same point of view in the law of his own country and there also punished with death. Gill draws the negative consequence for the woman, that nothing whatever is to be done to her, neither fine nor stripes and much less death, and notes of the earlier case that the parties were brought to the gate of the city where the thing was done, which one Aramaic version explains as the gate of the court of judicature in that city.
28:
Two of them supply a payment the text does not mention. Gill says the fifty shekels went to the father for the abuse of his daughter, and that besides this the man was obliged to give her her dowry as well, which Philo reports and which is commonly reckoned at fifty more; Wesley cites the same authority and explains the silence, that the dowry is omitted here because it was customary, it being sufficient to mention what was peculiar to this case. Wesley then adds a condition of his own to the marriage, that she becomes his wife if her father consented to it. Gill notes that the man is supposed to be unmarried, as appears from what follows, and Keil states the sentence plainly: because he has humbled her she is to be his wife, and he may not put her away all his days.

Keil raises a question about the last verse that is not about its sense but its place. Renewing as it does the prohibition of incest by repeating the first provision of the earlier law, he judges it no doubt much better adapted to close the laws of chastity and marriage than to introduce the laws which follow — the division of the chapters having put it at the head of the next.

How far that single prohibition reaches is disputed. Clarke keeps it narrow and concrete: it is to be understood of a stepmother, since a man in his old age may have married a young wife whom, at his death, his son by a former wife might wish to espouse; and he suggests it was probably on pretence of a breach of this law that Solomon put Adonijah to death for desiring his father's concubine. Gill collects the wider readings — a man's own mother or a stepmother, or, as one commentator thinks, any woman his father had known, or, as another has it, his father's brother's wife — and treats the clause as a sample of all the rest forbidden elsewhere, quoting the description of it as a short memorandum to make them careful of the whole law of incest. Calvin argues the opposite way from the same silence: since Moses refers to no other kind of incest here but speaks only of the stepmother, it is probable that what he had set forth more fully before he is now briefly recalling under a single head — and he adds the warning that prohibiting one offence does not open the gate to other abominations.

The second clause is read three ways. Gill takes the skirt for the token of marriage, of a woman over whom the father had thrown his skirt, so that both halves of the verse forbid the same thing. Wesley separates them, the first respecting the state of marriage and the second the act only. Calvin reads it as shame rather than marriage, the father being exposed when a stepson has no regard to decency, and wonders whether there is an allusion to the sin of Ham, who betrayed his ungodliness by uncovering his father.
